name: Lemborexant (DayVigo)
summary: Nighttime sleep medication for insomnia that helps with falling asleep and staying asleep by turning down the brain’s wake signal (orexin). Works fast, but can cause next-day drowsiness—especially at 10 mg or if you don’t get a full 7+ hours.
description: DayVigo is an orexin receptor antagonist used for adult insomnia (sleep onset and/or sleep maintenance). Most people take it only at bedtime, and only when they can commit to at least 7 hours before waking. It can work quickly (often within 15–20 minutes), but sedation and balance impairment can spill into the next day—particularly at 10 mg, in older adults, or when combined with other sedatives or alcohol. Rarely, it can trigger complex sleep behaviors (sleep-walking, sleep-driving) or narcolepsy-like effects (sleep paralysis, vivid hallucinations, cataplexy-like episodes).
patient_summary: DayVigo is a bedtime insomnia med that helps you fall asleep and stay asleep by blocking orexin (the brain’s “stay awake” signal). It can kick in fast, but the tradeoff is next-day drowsiness or fogginess—especially at 10 mg or if you don’t get a full night of sleep. Avoid alcohol and other sedatives. If you ever have sleep-walking/sleep-driving or scary sleep paralysis/hallucinations, stop and call your prescriber.

primary_indications: Insomnia (sleep onset and/or sleep maintenance) in adults

linked_conditions.context: FDA-labeled for insomnia when the core problem is trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or both. Best outcomes usually happen when it’s paired with CBT-I and sleep scheduling, not used as the only tool.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to lemborexant or any component of the formulation (explicitly listed in Canadian labeling)

efficacy_response.metric: Sleep onset and sleep maintenance in insomnia
efficacy_response.patient_text: DayVigo is designed to help with both falling asleep and staying asleep. In real-world use, people often notice faster sleep onset and fewer middle-of-the-night wake-ups, but the benefits are dose- and sleep-schedule-dependent: if you take it too late or don’t allow a full night of sleep, next-day impairment becomes much more likely.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Food can slow it down. A high-fat/high-calorie meal lowers the peak level, slightly increases overall exposure, and can delay the time to peak by about 2 hours—meaning it may take longer to kick in.
pharmacokinetics.onset: Rapid. Sleep onset is often within ~15 to 20 minutes in adult data; in adults ≥55 years, onset is commonly reported in the ~23 to 28 minute range.
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: About 1 to 3 hours (can be later if taken with/after a heavy meal).
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 (and to a lesser extent CYP3A5). Major active circulating metabolite: M10. Also a minor P-glycoprotein substrate. Weak inducer of CYP2B6.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Feces ~57%; urine ~29% (less than 1% as unchanged drug).
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: High-fat/high-calorie meals can delay effect and push the peak later; taking it with or soon after a meal can make sleep onset less predictable.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: DayVigo is for adult insomnia when the problem is falling asleep, staying asleep, or both. It’s not an “all day calm” medication—it’s strictly a bedtime sleep tool. For most people, it works best when you treat insomnia like a whole package: CBT-I and sleep habits first, meds as a targeted add-on when you actually need them.
items: {link:condition:insomnia:Insomnia}: Trouble falling asleep (sleep onset), staying asleep (sleep maintenance), or both
Short-term or intermittent support: Nights when insomnia is flaring and you can commit to a full night of sleep (≥7 hours)
Adjunct to CBT-I: Medication support while behavioral treatment is unavailable, ineffective, or not enough on its own

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: This is the vibe people describe most often. It’s not everyone, but it’s common enough that you should recognize it quickly:

quotes: It didn’t knock me out—it just made sleep feel easier to slide into.
My brain stopped fighting bedtime so hard.
I got sleepy in a normal way instead of wired-and-tired.
I wasn’t waking up every hour to check the clock.
Middle-of-the-night wakeups were shorter and less dramatic.
I still woke up sometimes, but I could fall back asleep.

items.category: Next-day fog (especially at 10 mg or short sleep)
quotes: The sleep was better, but the next morning felt heavy.
I could function, but I felt slower—like my brain had a delay.
If I took it too late, the next day was a mess.
items.note: Daytime impairment is much more likely if you don’t get a full night of sleep (under ~7 hours), if you go above 5 mg, or if you mix it with other sedatives.

quotes: I had vivid dreams that felt too real.
I had sleep paralysis and it freaked me out.
It felt like my body was asleep but my brain was awake.
items.note: Sleep paralysis, hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations, and cataplexy-like episodes have been reported. If it’s scary or unsafe, stop and call your prescriber.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: DayVigo is built for bedtime. It can work quickly, but the timing matters: food can delay it, and the sedating effects can linger—especially if you take it too late, don’t sleep long enough, or are sensitive to sedation.
key_points: ~15–20 minutes: Many people start drifting toward sleep (timing varies person-to-person)
~23–28 minutes: Typical reported sleep-onset timing in adults ≥55 years in cited data
1–3 hours: Peak blood levels (later if taken with/after a heavy meal)
At least 7 hours: Minimum sleep window you should plan for before waking
17–19 hours: Approximate half-life, which helps explain why next-day effects can happen in some people

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: DayVigo targets insomnia from a different angle than older hypnotics: it reduces the brain’s “stay awake” drive instead of directly amplifying sedation pathways. In practice, people often notice easier sleep onset and fewer/shorter awakenings—especially when the medication is taken correctly (bedtime only, no alcohol, and a full night available).
sections.clinical_details: Clinical data referenced in your notes describe rapid sleep onset in many users and sustained benefit over long-term follow-up in at least one 1-year study. The clinical takeaway is less about “stronger is better” and more about choosing the lowest effective dose—because next-day impairment and fall risk rise with higher dosing, short sleep windows, and combinations with other sedatives.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Do not take DayVigo unless you can sleep at least 7 hours. Avoid alcohol and other sedatives. Higher doses raise the risk of next-day impairment and falls.
other: Next-day drowsiness and slowed reaction time can happen, especially at 10 mg, in older adults, or when sleep time is shortened
Nighttime balance impairment has been observed; fall risk matters most in older adults and anyone who gets up at night
Rare complex sleep behaviors can occur (sleep-walking, sleep-driving, cooking/eating, phone calls, sex while asleep), sometimes with no memory afterward
Narcolepsy-like symptoms can occur: sleep paralysis, vivid hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations, and cataplexy-like episodes

Depression: hypnotics have been associated with worsening mood, suicidal thinking, and intentional overdose risk in vulnerable patients—use the smallest effective dose and prescribe the smallest quantity consistent with good care
Respiratory disease: use caution in sleep apnea, COPD, or respiratory compromise
If insomnia doesn’t improve after 7–10 days, don’t just keep escalating—re-evaluate for medical or psychiatric drivers of sleep disturbance
patient_counseling: Take it only at bedtime, and only when you have at least 7 hours before you need to be awake and functioning.
Avoid alcohol completely while using DayVigo. Alcohol can amplify sedation, memory issues, and balance problems.
Don’t combine with other sedating meds unless your prescriber specifically planned it (benzodiazepines, opioids, antihistamines like diphenhydramine, sleep meds, muscle relaxants, cannabis, etc.).
If you feel foggy or slow the next morning, don’t drive until you know how you respond—especially with the 10 mg dose.
If you or anyone notices sleep-walking/sleep-driving or other complex sleep behaviors, stop the medication and contact your prescriber immediately.
If you have frightening sleep paralysis, hallucinations around sleep, or cataplexy-like episodes, stop and call your prescriber.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: drowsiness and fatigue. Some people get headaches or vivid dreams/nightmares. Rarely, complex sleep behaviors and narcolepsy-like effects can happen (sleep paralysis, hallucinations, cataplexy-like symptoms).
plain_language_list: Sleep paralysis (rare but noticeable when it happens)

common.patient_note: This is the big one. Risk increases with 10 mg, taking it too late, sleeping less than ~7 hours, older age, and combining with other sedatives. If you feel impaired the next day, don’t drive and talk to your prescriber about dose reduction.
Some people describe this as a heavy, low-energy next day rather than pure sleepiness. If it’s persistent, consider stepping down to 5 mg, tightening your sleep schedule, and avoiding late dosing.
Usually mild. If headaches cluster around nights with short sleep or late dosing, timing is often part of the problem.
Vivid dreams can be tolerable or annoying depending on the person. If it becomes distressing or triggers anxiety about sleep, that’s a valid reason to adjust or switch.

This can feel intense: awake mind, body won’t move, lasts minutes. If it happens, it often shows up early in treatment (sometimes within the first 1–2 doses). Let your prescriber know—especially if it’s frightening.

serious: Complex sleep behaviors (rare): sleep-walking, sleep-driving, cooking/eating, phone calls, sex while asleep, often with amnesia afterward. Stop the medication and contact your prescriber immediately.
Severe next-day impairment: dangerous driving impairment has been reported in some patients, particularly with 10 mg. Do not drive until you know your response.
Narcolepsy-like effects (rare): hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations, cataplexy-like episodes. Stop and call your prescriber if these occur.
Worsening depression, suicidal thinking, or intentional overdose risk in vulnerable patients: use the smallest effective dose and close monitoring.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: DayVigo is mainly metabolized by CYP3A4, so strong CYP3A4 inhibitors can raise levels and increase sedation and next-day impairment. Alcohol and other sedatives are the most dangerous combo clinically.

items.risk: Increases CNS depression, daytime impairment, postural instability, and memory impairment.
items.action: Avoid alcohol completely while taking DayVigo.

items.with: Other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antihistamines, sleep meds, muscle relaxants, cannabis)
items.risk: Additive sedation and impaired coordination; higher fall risk and higher risk of next-day impairment.
items.action: Avoid combinations when possible. If a combo is medically necessary, use the lowest effective doses and counsel hard on safety (no driving, fall precautions).

items.with: Strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (examples: azole antifungals, macrolide antibiotics, certain antivirals)
items.risk: Higher lemborexant exposure and increased sedation/impairment risk.
items.action: Dose adjustment or avoidance may be needed. If you’re on interacting meds, treat DayVigo dosing as a prescriber-level decision, not a DIY adjustment.

items.with: CYP3A4 inducers (examples: rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John’s Wort)
items.risk: Lower lemborexant levels and reduced effectiveness; more insomnia breakthrough.
items.action: Avoid if possible. If the inducer is necessary, consider a different insomnia strategy.

items.risk: Delayed onset and later peak effect; the timing becomes less predictable.
items.action: If you need it to work quickly, don’t take it with or right after a heavy meal.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: DayVigo is not a benzodiazepine, and it is not typically tapered the way benzos are. Many people can stop without a formal taper. That said, if you’ve been taking it nightly for a long time, some people notice rebound insomnia (your sleep feels worse for a few nights) just because your brain got used to a medication-assisted bedtime. If you want a smoother landing, you can step down the dose or shift to intermittent use while you strengthen CBT-I skills and sleep scheduling.
key_points: Most patients do not require a taper, but rebound insomnia can happen when any sleep med is stopped after consistent nightly use.
A gentle step-down option: reduce from 10 mg to 5 mg for a period, then transition to intermittent use (only on the toughest nights).
Pair discontinuation with behavioral tools (CBT-I, consistent wake time, light exposure, stimulus control) to prevent the “med-free crash.”
If insomnia persists beyond 7–10 days despite appropriate use, reassess for medical/psychiatric drivers instead of escalating doses or stacking sedatives.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: DayVigo is a bedtime-only medication. The goal is the lowest dose that gets you to sleep without wrecking the next day. Most adults start at 5 mg at bedtime when needed, with at least 7 hours before waking. If 5 mg isn’t enough and you tolerate it well, some people go to 10 mg. Max is 10 mg/day.

adult.sleep_initial: 5 mg PO once nightly at bedtime as needed, with at least 7 hours before planned awakening
adult.sleep_titration: May increase to 10 mg at bedtime based on response and tolerability (watch for next-day impairment)
adult.prn_use: 5 mg PO at bedtime as needed (most people start here); only use on nights you can commit to a full night of sleep (≥7 hours)
adult.elderly: Use adult dosing, but be cautious with doses >5 mg due to higher risk of next-day sedation, balance impairment, and falls
adult.hepatic: Mild impairment: no adjustment. Moderate impairment: maximum 5 mg/day. Severe impairment: use not recommended (not studied).
adult.renal: Mild/moderate impairment: no adjustment. Severe impairment: no adjustment, but exposure may be higher and somnolence risk may increase—use extra caution.

sections.simple_explanation: Think of DayVigo as a “wake switch blocker.” You take it at bedtime only, and it helps your brain stop pushing wakefulness. The most common mistake is taking it too late or not allowing enough sleep time—then it works, but you pay for it the next day.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Pregnancy and breastfeeding data are limited. Lemborexant crosses the placenta, and it is present in human milk. If you’re pregnant, trying to conceive, or breastfeeding, the risk/benefit conversation should be explicit—especially because non-medication insomnia treatments (CBT-I) are often highly effective and safer.
sections.pregnancy: Lemborexant crosses the placenta and outcome data in pregnancy are limited. If exposure occurs, consider enrolling in the National Pregnancy Registry for Psychiatric Medications (1-866-961-2388; womensmentalhealth.org/research/pregnancyregistry). Use the smallest effective dose and avoid poly-sedation whenever possible.
sections.lactation: Lemborexant is present in breast milk. Case reports and small studies estimate a relative infant dose (RID) around ~1% to ~2% of the weight-adjusted maternal dose in available data, which is generally below the commonly used 10% threshold. Even with a low RID, practical risk still exists because this medication can reduce alertness. If used during breastfeeding, monitor the infant for excessive sedation and feeding issues, and discuss timing/avoidance strategies with a clinician.
sections.pediatrics: Not applicable for this medication. Safety and efficacy in pediatric patients are not established.
sections.geriatrics: Use adult dosing but lean conservative. Doses above 5 mg increase the risk of next-day sedation, night-time balance impairment, and falls—especially if the patient gets up to use the bathroom at night or is on other sedatives.
sections.hepatic: Moderate hepatic impairment: do not exceed 5 mg/day. Severe hepatic impairment: not recommended because it has not been studied and exposure may be higher.
sections.renal: No formal dose adjustment is required, but patients with severe renal impairment may have increased exposure and a higher chance of somnolence—so the safety margin is tighter.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Next-day impairment: morning sleepiness, slowed reaction time, cognitive fog, driving impairment (especially with 10 mg or short sleep windows).
Falls and balance: night-time unsteadiness, particularly in older adults or anyone who gets up at night.
Mood changes: worsening depression, suicidal thoughts, irritability, emotional flattening—especially in patients with baseline depression.
Complex sleep behaviors: any sleep-walking, sleep-driving, cooking/eating while asleep, phone calls, sex while asleep, or amnesia for events.
Narcolepsy-like symptoms: sleep paralysis, hallucinations around sleep, cataplexy-like episodes.
Sedative stacking: review alcohol use and other CNS depressants at every visit.
Hepatic and renal function: baseline and as clinically indicated, especially in known impairment or when sedation is unexpectedly strong.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: DayVigo is available as tablets. There is no generic equivalent listed in your notes.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: DayVigo blocks orexin A and orexin B from binding to OX1R and OX2R receptors. Orexin is one of the brain’s main “stay awake” systems. By turning that signal down, DayVigo suppresses wake drive and makes sleep easier to initiate and maintain.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: DayVigo fits best as a targeted insomnia medication when CBT-I isn’t available, hasn’t worked well enough, or you need additional support for a period of time. Clinically, the main skill is dosing discipline: bedtime only, full night available, avoid sedative stacking. Compared with older hypnotics, orexin antagonists are conceptually more about reducing wakefulness than forcing sedation—but the real-world safety issues still revolve around next-day impairment, falls, and rare complex sleep behaviors. If sleep isn’t improving after about a week of appropriate use, it’s a sign to re-check the diagnosis (depression, anxiety, PTSD nightmares, sleep apnea, restless legs, circadian misalignment, substance use) rather than simply increasing the dose or adding more sedatives.

seo.title: Lemborexant (DayVigo): Uses, Dosage, Side Effects & Next-Day Drowsiness
seo.description: DayVigo (lemborexant) for insomnia: bedtime dosing (5–10 mg), how fast it works, common side effects (drowsiness, fatigue, vivid dreams), rare complex sleep behaviors, interactions (alcohol/sedatives), and special considerations for pregnancy and breastfeeding.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: DayVigo (lemborexant) is used to treat insomnia in adults—meaning trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or both. It’s a bedtime-only medication, not a daytime anxiety medication.

In the data referenced in your notes, sleep onset is often around 15–20 minutes, with somewhat slower onset in adults ≥55 (around the mid-20 minute range). In real life, the timing varies—especially if you take it with or soon after a heavy meal, which can delay the effect.

faqs.q: What’s the usual DayVigo dose for insomnia?
faqs.a: Most adults start with 5 mg by mouth at bedtime as needed, only when they can sleep at least 7 hours before waking. If 5 mg isn’t enough and it’s well tolerated, some people increase to 10 mg. Maximum is 10 mg per day.

faqs.q: Why does DayVigo make some people feel drowsy the next day?
faqs.a: DayVigo blocks orexin (the brain’s wake signal). If you don’t get a full night of sleep, take it too late, use 10 mg, or combine it with other sedatives or alcohol, that “wake suppression” can spill into the next morning as fogginess, slowed reaction time, or driving impairment.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol with DayVigo?
faqs.a: No. Alcohol increases CNS depression, daytime impairment, postural instability, and memory impairment with lemborexant. It’s one of the highest-risk combos because it directly stacks sedation and coordination problems.

faqs.q: What are complex sleep behaviors, and can DayVigo cause them?
faqs.a: Complex sleep behaviors are activities you do while not fully awake—like sleep-walking, sleep-driving, cooking/eating, phone calls, or sex while asleep—often with no memory afterward. They’re rare but have been reported with lemborexant, even at therapeutic doses, with or without alcohol/other sedatives. If this happens, stop the medication and contact your prescriber immediately.

faqs.q: Can DayVigo cause sleep paralysis or hallucinations?
faqs.a: Yes, infrequently. Sleep paralysis (can’t move or speak during sleep-wake transitions), hallucinations around sleep onset or waking, and even cataplexy-like episodes have been reported. If it’s frightening, unsafe, or persistent, stop and talk to your prescriber.

faqs.q: Is DayVigo safe for older adults?
faqs.a: It can be used, but with extra caution. Older adults are more sensitive to sedation and balance impairment, which raises fall risk. Your notes recommend using adult dosing but being cautious with doses above 5 mg.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper off DayVigo?
faqs.a: Usually no. DayVigo is not typically tapered the way benzodiazepines are. Some people can still experience rebound insomnia after stopping any sleep medication if they’ve been taking it nightly, so a step-down (10 mg → 5 mg → intermittent use) can make the transition smoother for some patients.

faqs.q: What if DayVigo doesn’t work after a week?
faqs.a: If insomnia isn’t improving after about 7–10 days of appropriate use, it’s a sign to re-evaluate what’s driving the sleep problem (depression, anxiety, PTSD nightmares, sleep apnea, restless legs, circadian timing, substances, medications) rather than just increasing dose or stacking more sedatives.

faqs.q: Can I take DayVigo if I have liver or kidney problems?
faqs.a: Kidney impairment: no formal dose adjustment is required, but severe impairment may increase exposure and somnolence risk—so the safety margin is tighter. Liver impairment: mild impairment generally needs no adjustment; moderate impairment should not exceed 5 mg/day; severe impairment is not recommended because it hasn’t been studied.

faqs.q: Is DayVigo safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Data are limited. Lemborexant crosses the placenta. It is present in human milk, with small studies/case reports estimating infant exposure (RID) roughly in the ~1% to ~2% range in cited calculations. Even with low estimated exposure, infants should be monitored for sedation if it’s used during breastfeeding. If exposure occurs in pregnancy, enrollment in the National Pregnancy Registry for Psychiatric Medications is encouraged.
Yes. Your notes list lemborexant (DayVigo) as a Schedule IV controlled substance.
